newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian Q3 inflation data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian Q3 inflation data.

text.p: Australia's consumer price index rose 0.3 percent in the September quarter to be 2.1 percent higher over the past year, official figures show.
The underlying rate of inflation rose 0.5 percent in the quarter, to be 2.4 percent higher over the past year.

Median forecasts had been for the CPI to rise 0.3 percent in the quarter and 2.2 percent over the year. The underlying rate was seen rising 0.6 percent and 2.5 percent over the year. A selection of immediate reactions to the data follows.
SUSAN CREIGTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ABN AMRO:

"Well, obviously a very very good result. Unambiguously good number I'd say on the face of it. It's obviously telling us that the beniegn inflation environment in the economy has continued through the September quarter. It's very important that the underlying inflation reading has got back in the RBA's two to three percent range, and as the RBA itself has said, it's highly likely that underlying inflation will stay in that two to three percent range for quite some time. The risk to that over coming quarters does lie in what happens on the wages, and of course that is the big question for tomorrow."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP INVESTMENTS:

"The figures were basically neutral for the market. We have now seen underlying inflation fall back to well within the (Reserve Bank of Australia's) two to three percent target range. Given that, and expectations that wages growth will gradually slow, that would all be consistent with an easing. I think it really confirms the market's expectation that there can be an easing."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"It's a good number which puts the underlying inflation rate in the bottom half of the Reserve Bank's target range and, provided that tomorrow's wages number is within the Reserve Banks's comfort zone, then there's still a good chance of a rate cut before Christmas ...I still think the odds of a rate cut before Christmas are a touch better than 50-50."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"This is clearly a pretty good number. It is in line with our forecasts. We were expecting a pretty good outcome for underlying infation, and that's been affirming our view that we still have scope for an interest rate cut this year. It will still depend on the wages numbers tomorrow, but if they come out in line with expectations, another good number, it's going to be hard for the Reserve Bank really to not be cutting rates, maybe as early as November."
MATTHEW DRENNAN, ECONOMIST, AXIOM FUNDS MANAGEMENT:

"The headline CPI was pretty much in line with expectations. The underlying was a little bit deader than people were expecting. But I still think a good inflation outcome is insufficient to guarantee an easing in monetary policy. You need the Reserve Bank also to be comfortable that wages, particularly enterprise agreements, are growing at around about five percent and there's no sign of that at present. You also need the bank to believe that the economy as a whole is going to grow below trend and I don't think they believe that yet either. It's still pretty difficult to see them moving after the November meeting."
IVAN COLHOUN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BAIN AND CO:

"It was probably the least reaction I can remember to a CPI number, the high/low today is a five point range on the 10-year bonds. That says it didn't surprise anyone particularly and you would have to say that because the headline is basically around expectations, probably a bit at the low end, and underlying was a bit below. Would they (the RBA) be surprised by this? No. What are they concerned about, if you listen to what they have been saying, is they are more concerned about wages. I would say it is a very good number. Inflation is not our problem at the moment in the short term."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"A pretty good result. Pretty much as expected, even amongst the components. All pretty much as expected and as a result the market has not done too much on it. The big focus is on tomorrow's wages number, and the wild card in all of this is still the enterprise bargaining agreements. Today's data would not stand on the way of a rate cut, but it doesn't make one inevitable either."
ANTHONY THOMPSON, ECONOMIST HONGKONGBANK AUSTRALIA:

"Obviously it's encouraging that we are well into the 2.0 to 3.0 percent target range in the underlying measure. Another thing that encourages me for the outlook for a rate cut is that the fall in mortgage interest charges wasn't as great as I had forecast. It seems as if still there is going to be more impact on the negative through mortgage cuts on the headline rate in the December quarter from the rate cut in July."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
